claim: Long-term in vivo antigenic exposure induced a specific deficit in numerous metabolic enzymes in T cells.
source: Here, we report that long-term in vivo antigenic exposure induced a specific deficit in numerous metabolic enzymes.
evidence: Supported by proteomic analysis showing down-regulation of metabolic enzymes in chronic T cells (Table 1)

claim: Chronic T cells exhibited low basal glycolytic flux.
source: Accordingly, T cells exhibited low basal glycolytic flux and limited respiratory capacity.
evidence: Supported by ECAR measurements shown in Figure 3A

claim: Chronic T cells exhibited limited respiratory capacity.
source: Accordingly, T cells exhibited low basal glycolytic flux and limited respiratory capacity.
evidence: Supported by OCR measurements shown in Figure 3A

claim: Blockade of inhibitory receptor PD-1 stimulated the production of IFNγ in chronic T cells.
source: Strikingly, blockade of inhibitory receptor PD-1 stimulated the production of IFNγ in chronic T cells, but failed to shift their metabolism towards aerobic glycolysis, as observed in effector T cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C and 2B

claim: PD-1 blockade failed to shift chronic T cell metabolism towards aerobic glycolysis.
source: Strikingly, blockade of inhibitory receptor PD-1 stimulated the production of IFNγ in chronic T cells, but failed to shift their metabolism towards aerobic glycolysis, as observed in effector T cells.
evidence: Supported by metabolic measurements in Figure 5B showing no increase in ECAR after PD-1 blockade

claim: Chronic T cells rely on oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) to produce ATP for IFNγ synthesis.
source: Instead, chronic T cells appeared to rely on oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and fatty acid oxidation (FAO) to produce ATP for IFNγ synthesis.
evidence: Supported by oligomycin inhibition experiments shown in Figure 4A and 4B

claim: Chronic T cells rely on fatty acid oxidation (FAO) to produce ATP for IFNγ synthesis.
source: Instead, chronic T cells appeared to rely on oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and fatty acid oxidation (FAO) to produce ATP for IFNγ synthesis.
evidence: Supported by Etomoxir inhibition experiments shown in Figure 4A

claim: Check-point blockade increased mitochondrial production of superoxide in chronic T cells.
source: Check-point blockade, however, increased mitochondrial production of superoxide and reduced viability and effector function.
evidence: Supported by MitoSOX measurements in Pdcd1-/- T cells shown in Figure 6A

claim: Check-point blockade reduced viability of chronic T cells.
source: Check-point blockade, however, increased mitochondrial production of superoxide and reduced viability and effector function.
evidence: Supported by viability data shown in Figure 6C and 6D

claim: PD-1-mediated inhibition is essential for limiting oxidative metabolism linked to effector function in chronic T cells.
source: Thus, in the absence of a glycolytic switch, PD-1-mediated inhibition appears essential for limiting oxidative metabolism linked to effector function in chronic T cells, thereby promoting survival and functional fitness.
evidence: Supported by comparison of Pdcd1+/+ and Pdcd1-/- chronic T cells showing higher OCR and ROS in Pdcd1-/- cells (Figures 5C, 6A)

claim: PD-1-mediated inhibition promotes survival of chronic T cells.
source: Thus, in the absence of a glycolytic switch, PD-1-mediated inhibition appears essential for limiting oxidative metabolism linked to effector function in chronic T cells, thereby promoting survival and functional fitness.
evidence: Supported by reduced viability in Pdcd1-/- chronic T cells (Figure 6C, 6D)

claim: PD-1-mediated inhibition promotes functional fitness of chronic T cells.
source: Thus, in the absence of a glycolytic switch, PD-1-mediated inhibition appears essential for limiting oxidative metabolism linked to effector function in chronic T cells, thereby promoting survival and functional fitness.
evidence: Supported by NAC rescue experiments showing improved IFNγ production (Figure 7A, 7B)

claim: Quiescent T cells rely on oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) for energy production.
source: Quiescent T cells rely on oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) for energy production (Plas et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Plas et al., 2002

claim: Activated T cells shift from oxidative metabolism to a highly glycolytic and glutamine-dependent metabolic program.
source: However, once activated by foreign antigens, they shift from an energetically efficient oxidative metabolism to a highly glycolytic and glutamine-dependent metabolic program (Chang et al., 2013; Nakaya et al., 2014; Gubser et al., 2013; van der Windt et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Chang et al., 2013; Nakaya et al., 2014; Gubser et al., 2013; van der Windt et al., 2013

claim: The metabolic switch to glycolysis endows T cells with the capacity to direct metabolic intermediates toward synthesis of macromolecules required for proliferation and effector function.
source: This metabolic switch endows T cells with the capacity to direct rapidly metabolic intermediates toward the synthesis of macromolecules required for proliferation and effector function.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about metabolic reprogramming in activated T cells

claim: T cells can rely on OXPHOS alone to become activated and proliferate when aerobic glycolysis is impaired.
source: Interestingly, when aerobic glycolysis is impaired, T cells can also rely on OXPHOS alone to become activated and proliferate (Chang et al., 2013; Sena et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chang et al., 2013; Sena et al., 2013

claim: When T cells rely on OXPHOS alone, their effector function is compromised with impaired cytokine production.
source: In this case, T cell effector function is compromised, with impaired cytokine production caused by posttranscriptional regulation of glycolytic enzymes (Chang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chang et al., 2013

claim: Aerobic glycolysis allows for the acquisition of full effector functions in activated T cells.
source: Thus, in addition to providing precursors for biomass production in activated T cells, aerobic glycolysis allows for the acquisition of full effector functions.
evidence: Based on inference from previous statements and cited literature

claim: The capacity of T cells to limit glycolysis has been linked to the expression of the cell surface inhibitory receptor PD-1.
source: The capacity of T cells to limit glycolysis has been linked to the expression of the cell surface inhibitory receptor PD-1 (2), which is increased following T cell activation (Agata et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Agata et al., 1996

claim: PD-1 expression is increased following T cell activation.
source: The capacity of T cells to limit glycolysis has been linked to the expression of the cell surface inhibitory receptor PD-1 (2), which is increased following T cell activation (Agata et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Agata et al., 1996

claim: The function of inhibitory receptors such as PD-1 is to attenuate signaling downstream of the TcR.
source: The function of inhibitory receptors such as PD-1 is to attenuate signaling downstream of the TcR, leading to suppression of T-cell proliferation, cytokine production and cytolytic function (Yokosuka et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yokosuka et al., 2012

claim: PD-1 signaling leads to suppression of T-cell proliferation, cytokine production and cytolytic function.
source: The function of inhibitory receptors such as PD-1 is to attenuate signaling downstream of the TcR, leading to suppression of T-cell proliferation, cytokine production and cytolytic function (Yokosuka et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yokosuka et al., 2012

claim: PD-1 signaling regulates T cell function by inhibiting glycolysis.
source: Recently, PD-1 signaling was shown to regulate T cell function by inhibiting glycolysis (Patsoukis et al., 2015; Bengsch et al., 2016), and to promote T cell survival through lipolysis and OXPHOS fueled by fatty acids (Patsoukis et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Patsoukis et al., 2015; Bengsch et al., 2016

claim: PD-1 promotes T cell survival through lipolysis and OXPHOS fueled by fatty acids.
source: Recently, PD-1 signaling was shown to regulate T cell function by inhibiting glycolysis (Patsoukis et al., 2015; Bengsch et al., 2016), and to promote T cell survival through lipolysis and OXPHOS fueled by fatty acids (Patsoukis et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Patsoukis et al., 2015

claim: Most cases of SCID are due to mutations in the gene encoding common gamma chain (γc).
source: Most cases of SCID are due to mutations in the gene encoding common gamma chain (γc), a protein shared by several receptors for interleukins IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15 and IL-21 (Malek et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Malek et al., 1999

claim: Common gamma chain (γc) is a protein shared by several receptors for interleukins IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15 and IL-21.
source: Most cases of SCID are due to mutations in the gene encoding common gamma chain (γc), a protein shared by several receptors for interleukins IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15 and IL-21 (Malek et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Malek et al., 1999

claim: Mutations in γc resulting in expression defects cause complete absence of adaptive immunity.
source: Because these cytokines are needed for T cell development, mutations resulting in expression defects cause complete absence of adaptive immunity (Fischer et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fischer et al., 2015

claim: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) transplantation is the only available treatment for SCID.
source: Currently, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) transplantation is the only available treatment for SCID.
evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge

claim: Recipient-specific donor T cells present in the graft can cause persistent chronic graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) in allogeneic HSC-transplanted SCID patients.
source: However, recipient-specific donor T cells present in the graft can cause significant inflammatory events in allogeneic HSC-transplanted SCID patients, including persistent chronic graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) (Neven et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Neven et al., 2009

claim: PD-1 contributes to the suppression of T cell-mediated GVHD in experimental animals transplanted with HSC after myeloablative treatment.
source: In experimental animals transplanted with HSC after myeloablative treatment, PD-1 was shown to contribute to the suppression of T cell-mediated GVHD, and PD-1 blockade was associated with an increased glycolytic metabolism in GVHD T cells (Saha et al., 2013; Fujiwara et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Saha et al., 2013; Fujiwara et al., 2014

claim: PD-1 blockade is associated with an increased glycolytic metabolism in GVHD T cells in experimental animals.
source: In experimental animals transplanted with HSC after myeloablative treatment, PD-1 was shown to contribute to the suppression of T cell-mediated GVHD, and PD-1 blockade was associated with an increased glycolytic metabolism in GVHD T cells (Saha et al., 2013; Fujiwara et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Saha et al., 2013; Fujiwara et al., 2014

claim: The relative number of donor T cells present in the recipient's spleen increased with time after transfer.
source: Though the relative number of donor T cells present in the recipient's spleen increased with time, their absolute numbers were similar at 6 to 21 days post-transfer (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The absolute numbers of donor T cells were similar at 6 to 21 days post-transfer.
source: Though the relative number of donor T cells present in the recipient's spleen increased with time, their absolute numbers were similar at 6 to 21 days post-transfer (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Most T cells were activated after transfer, as indicated by their expression pattern of CD44 and CD62L.
source: After transfer, most T cells were activated, as indicated by their expression pattern of CD44 and CD62L, and expressed PD-1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Transferred T cells expressed PD-1.
source: After transfer, most T cells were activated, as indicated by their expression pattern of CD44 and CD62L, and expressed PD-1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B

claim: In vitro stimulation with irradiated allogeneic cells stimulated the production of IFNγ in both day 7 and day 21 T cell populations.
source: In vitro stimulation with irradiated allogeneic cells stimulated the production of IFNγ in both T cell populations (Figure 1C), and blockade of PD-1/PD-L1 interaction significantly increased the amount of cytokine produced, confirming that T cell-mediated GVHD is regulated by PD-1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Blockade of PD-1/PD-L1 interaction significantly increased the amount of IFNγ produced by T cells.
source: In vitro stimulation with irradiated allogeneic cells stimulated the production of IFNγ in both T cell populations (Figure 1C), and blockade of PD-1/PD-L1 interaction significantly increased the amount of cytokine produced, confirming that T cell-mediated GVHD is regulated by PD-1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1C

claim: T cell-mediated GVHD is regulated by PD-1.
source: In vitro stimulation with irradiated allogeneic cells stimulated the production of IFNγ in both T cell populations (Figure 1C), and blockade of PD-1/PD-L1 interaction significantly increased the amount of cytokine produced, confirming that T cell-mediated GVHD is regulated by PD-1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1C showing increased IFNγ after PD-1 blockade

claim: T cells produced higher amounts of IFNγ at day seven than after day 21.
source: We noticed, however, that T cells produced higher amounts of IFNγ at day seven than after day 21 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Day 6 T cells were highly sensitive to glycolysis inhibition by 2-DG.
source: Day 6 T cells were highly sensitive to glycolysis inhibition, whereas day 21 T cells were not inhibited (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by 2-DG inhibition data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Day 21 T cells were not inhibited by 2-DG.
source: Day 6 T cells were highly sensitive to glycolysis inhibition, whereas day 21 T cells were not inhibited (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by 2-DG inhibition data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Long-term antigen exposure up-regulated PD-1 expression on male-specific CD4+ T cells.
source: Long-term antigen exposure (21 days) up-regulated PD-1 expression on male-specific CD4+ T cells (Figure 2A).

claim: Spleen cells containing male-specific T cells and male APCs produced IFNγ after PD-1/PD-L1 blockade.
source: Spleen cells isolated from adoptively transferred recipients, which contained male-specific T cells and male APCs, produced IFNγ after PD-1/PD-L1 blockade (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2B

claim: IFNγ production after PD-1/PD-L1 blockade was the result of T cell activity.
source: Cytokine production was the result of T cell activity since IFNγ was not detected after blocking T cell antigen recognition (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by antibody blocking experiments shown in Figure 2B

claim: Engagement of PD-1 by immobilized PD-L1-Ig prevented IFNγ production in anti-CD3/CD28-stimulated purified chronic CD4+ T cells.
source: The capacity of PD-1 to inhibit T cell activity was further documented by the observation that engagement of PD-1 by immobilized PD-L1-Ig prevented IFNγ production in anti-CD3/CD28-stimulated purified chronic CD4+ T cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Blockade of PD-1/PD-L1 interaction decreased by one log the amount of male peptides required for T cell activation and IFNγ production.
source: Moreover, blockade of PD-1/PD-L1 interaction in an antigen-specific assay decreased by one log the amount of male peptides required for T cell activation and IFNγ production (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by peptide titration data shown in Figure 2D

claim: PD-1 is responsible for limiting the functional responsiveness of chronic anti-male CD4+ T cells by raising their TcR activation threshold.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrated that PD-1 is responsible for limiting the functional responsiveness of chronic anti-male CD4+ T cells, and that this regulation is carried out by raising their TcR activation threshold.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data in Figures 2B-D

claim: Injecting anti-PD-L1 antibodies to male recipients increased the number of T cells infiltrating liver, gut, skin and kidney.
source: Moreover, injecting anti-PD-L1 antibodies to male recipients increased sharply the number of T cells infiltrating several organs, such as liver, gut, skin and kidney (Figure 2E and data not shown), demonstrating that PD-1 also controlled in vivo the activity of chronic CD4+ T cells.
evidence: Supported by cell count data shown in Figure 2E

claim: PD-1 controls in vivo the activity of chronic CD4+ T cells.
source: Moreover, injecting anti-PD-L1 antibodies to male recipients increased sharply the number of T cells infiltrating several organs, such as liver, gut, skin and kidney (Figure 2E and data not shown), demonstrating that PD-1 also controlled in vivo the activity of chronic CD4+ T cells.
evidence: Supported by in vivo antibody treatment data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Purified chronic T cells were unable to proliferate when stimulated in vitro by anti-CD3/CD28 antibodies.
source: Importantly, when stimulated in vitro by anti-CD3/CD28 antibodies, purified chronic T cells were unable to proliferate (Figure 2F), suggesting that increased organ infiltration by T cells observed after anti-PD-L1 antibody treatment was not due to T cell proliferation but enhanced T cell recruitment.
evidence: Supported by CFSE proliferation data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Increased organ infiltration by T cells after anti-PD-L1 antibody treatment was not due to T cell proliferation but enhanced T cell recruitment.
source: Importantly, when stimulated in vitro by anti-CD3/CD28 antibodies, purified chronic T cells were unable to proliferate (Figure 2F), suggesting that increased organ infiltration by T cells observed after anti-PD-L1 antibody treatment was not due to T cell proliferation but enhanced T cell recruitment.

claim: Adding PD-L1-specific antibodies did not improve chronic T cells' capacity to produce IFNγ after anti-CD3/CD28 stimulation.
source: As seen in Figure 2G and H, adding PD-L1-specific antibodies did not improve T cells' capacity to produce IFNγ after activation.

claim: In in vitro experiments with purified T cells, PD-L1/CD80 interactions did not regulate the activity of chronic T cells.
source: These results demonstrated that, in our in vitro experiments, PD-L1/CD80 interactions did not regulate the activity of chronic T cells.
evidence: Based on inference from data in Figures 2G and 2H showing no effect of anti-PD-L1 on purified T cells

claim: Long term antigen exposure down-regulated transketolase (TKT) in CD4+ T cells.

claim: Basal glycolytic flux was high in control effector T cells.

claim: Basal glycolytic flux was similarly low in naive and chronic CD4+ T cells.
source: Basal glycolytic flux, assessed by measuring ECAR, was high in control effector T cells, but similarly low in naive and chronic CD4+ T cells (Figure 3A).

claim: Basal respiration was significantly higher in effector T cells compared to naive and chronic T cells.

claim: The spare respiratory capacity in chronic T cells was modest compared with naive or effector T cells.

claim: Chronic T cells have lower mitochondrial mass compared to effector T cells.

claim: Chronic T cells have a reduced capacity to synthesize ATP after activation.

claim: Chronic CD4+ T cells have a low energy metabolism and a reduced capacity to produce cellular energy.

claim: Following activation, naive T cells secreted large amount of IL-2 but failed to produce IFNγ in the absence of IL-12.

claim: After activation, effector T cells produced large quantities of both IL-2 and IFNγ.

claim: 2-DG only weakly inhibited IFNγ production by chronic T cells.

claim: During early chronic antigen stimulation, PD-1-mediated inhibition of TcR signaling creates bioenergetics deficiencies to control T cell function.
source: On the one hand, during early chronic antigen stimulation, PD-1-mediated inhibition of TcR signaling creates bioenergetics deficiencies to control T cell function.
evidence: Based on inference from day 7 T cell data

claim: Over prolonged antigen stimulation, PD-1 limits T cell oxidative metabolism in order to maintain functional fitness and cell survival.
source: By contrast, our data show that, over prolonged antigen stimulation, PD-1 limits T cell oxidative metabolism in order to maintain functional fitness and cell survival.
evidence: Based on inference from day 21 T cell data

claim: In chronic CD4+ T cells, IFNγ production is impaired by fast mRNA decay.
source: Moreover, we also show that in chronic CD4+ T cells IFNγ production is impaired by fast mRNA decay.
evidence: Supported by mRNA decay data in Figure 7E

claim: In chronic CD4+ T cells, PD-1 increases T cell activation threshold to prevent excessive RNA oxidation and decay.
source: Therefore, accumulation of RNA damage must be prevented and cells have developed specific mechanisms to remove oxidized RNA molecules (Li et al., 2006). Our data support the notion that, in chronic CD4+ T cells, PD-1 increases T cell activation threshold to prevent excessive RNA oxidation and decay, consequently preserving the capacity of T cells to produce inflammatory cytokines such as IFNγ.
evidence: Based on inference from ROS and mRNA decay data, with citation to Li et al., 2006

claim: Duration of antigen encounter modifies the different metabolic programs available to activated CD4+ T cells for supporting their function.
source: Overall, our data are consistent with the concept that duration of antigen encounter modifies the different metabolic programs available to activated CD4+ T cells for supporting their function.
evidence: Summary statement based on comparison of early and late chronic T cells

claim: Although early metabolic dysfunction is a characteristic of a plastic differentiation state, it ultimately becomes fixed and non-reversible.
source: Thus, although early metabolic dysfunction is still a characteristic of a plastic differentiation state, it ultimately becomes fixed and non-reversible.
evidence: Based on inference from time-course data and PD-1 blockade experiments

claim: Promoting PD-1-mediated regulation of T cell metabolism might represent an effective therapeutic tool for controlling the early steps of chronic immune pathologies.
source: Our study could have important implications for the control of T cell activity in chronic immune diseases. Our data support the possibility that promoting PD-1-mediated regulation of T cell metabolism might represent an effective therapeutic tool for controlling the early steps of chronic immune pathologies.
evidence: Based on speculation from study findings

claim: Blocking PD-1/PD-L1 interactions might face therapeutic limitations in attempting to restore the function of T cells submitted to long-term chronic antigen stimulation.
source: Paradoxically, they also enlighten the potential therapeutic limitations that blocking PD-1/PD-L1 interactions might face in attempting to restore the function of T cells submitted to long-term chronic antigen stimulation.
evidence: Based on speculation from study findings showing limited efficacy of PD-1 blockade in late chronic T cells
